newsitem.title: USA: Colonial wins okay to raise distillate throughput.
newsitem.headline: Colonial wins okay to raise distillate throughput.

text.p: Colonial Pipeline Co has won the right from federal regulators to resume pumping distillates on its refined products line to the maximum allowable level, Colonial and U.S. officials said.

"They released our pressure restriction," said Mel Coke, an operations manager at the Atlanta-based pipeline company. The restriction related to damage in June on part of the line in Simpsonville, S.C., which has since been repaired.

The decision, which was relayed to Colonial clients on Friday, enables the pipline company to pump up to 888,000 barrels per day of distillates like heating oil, does not relate to the allocation program Colonial imposed last week.

Colonial is still pro-rationing space on Houston-to-New York line amid a scramble by refiners and marketers to move heating oil up to the huge East Coast heating oil market, where stocks remain at historically low levels.
Federal officials said Colonial has not yet reached maximum allowed pumping pressure, but has indeed won federal approval to do so.
"We have allowed them to resume pumping at higher pressure," said Patricia Klinger, a spokeswoman at the U.S. Department of Transportation Office of Pipeline Safety.

The arterial Colonial Pipeline extends from Houston to Linden, N.J., on the edge of New York Harbor and includes a 1.2 million bpd gasoline line, which has been partly opened to distillates to help make up the East Coast stocks shortfall.

The 10 companies that make up the Colonial consortium include Amoco Corp, Atlantic Richfield Co, Citgo Petroleum Co, owned by Petroleos de Venezuela SA, Conoco Inc, a unit of DuPont Co, Mobil Corp, Phillips Petroleum Co, Texaxo Inc, Union Oil, a unit of Unocal Corp, and Marathon Oil Co, a unit of USX-Marathon Group.
